questions.question: Why can an Angular component show stale data after an object is mutated, and how do you fix it?
questions.title: Stale Views and Immutable State Updates
questions.direct_answer: A mutation changes fields inside an object without changing its reference. A signal using default equality may reject the same reference, and an OnPush child may not receive a new input notification, so its view can remain stale. Return a new object or array reference through the state API that Angular observes.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Object mutation changes contents but keeps the same reference.
Signal values use referential equality by default for objects and arrays.
An OnPush child is notified when it receives a new bound input value.
Use `signal.update(value => ({ ...value, field }))` for an object update.
Keep one state owner and send a replacement value across component boundaries.

sections.title: Interview answer
Reference identity at signal and input boundaries
sections.content:
Angular needs both a changed value and a reason to check the relevant view. An object mutation supplies neither by itself. The variable still points at the same object, and no Angular state API necessarily ran. A later click may trigger checking and reveal the mutation, but the original update path remains unreliable.

Signals make the boundary explicit. Calling `user.update(current => ({ ...current, name }))` creates a new object. Default signal equality sees a different reference and notifies consumers. If the signal is read in a template, Angular marks that view for checking. If its result is passed as an input, the child receives the replacement value.

Consider a profile editor and profile card. The editor owns the user signal. Saving a name creates a new user object while reusing unchanged fields. The card only renders its input. This avoids two owners changing the same object and makes a failed update easy to locate.

Copying has a cost for very large data structures, and blindly deep-cloning everything is not required. Replace only the changed path and preserve stable references for unchanged branches. A custom signal equality function is an advanced option, but it can hide meaningful changes if it is wrong. Clear ownership and shallow immutable updates are the safer default for fresher code.

sections.title: Mutation path and replacement path
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Old[Existing object reference] --> Mutate[Mutate a field]
  Mutate --> Same[Same reference]
  Same --> Miss[No signal or input change notification]
  Old --> Copy[Create object with changed field]
  Copy --> New[New reference]
  New --> Notify[Signal and input notification]
  Notify --> View[View binding updates]
```

questions.question: Why is `track` important when rendering a dynamic list with Angular `@for`?
questions.title: Stable Identity in Angular Lists
questions.direct_answer: `track` tells Angular which logical item owns each repeated view. A stable unique key such as `item.id` lets Angular reuse or move the correct DOM and component instance during inserts, deletes, and reorders instead of confusing item state or recreating the whole list.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `@for` uses `track` to match items with their existing views.
A stable unique database ID is usually the best tracking key.
Duplicate keys cannot identify two different items correctly.
`track $index` fits only collections whose positions do not change.
Tracking object identity can recreate views when fresh objects arrive from an API.

sections.title: Interview answer
Collection differences and repeated view ownership
sections.content:
Every `@for` item gets an embedded view containing its DOM nodes, local template variables, and any child component instances. When the collection changes, Angular must decide which old view corresponds to which new item. The tracking key supplies that answer.

Suppose tasks 10, 20, and 30 are displayed and the user is editing task 20. A new task 5 is inserted at the beginning. With `track task.id`, Angular knows that the editor view for 20 still belongs to task 20 and only its position changed. With index tracking, the old view at index one may now be associated with task 10, so position-based local state can follow the wrong logical item.

A useful key comes from data identity: a database primary key, immutable UUID, or another unique stable field. Display text is often a poor key because two items can share it and users can edit it. Random values are worse because every check invents new identities and prevents reuse.

Stable tracking does not make mutable collection updates automatically reactive. The collection owner must still publish a new signal value or otherwise notify Angular. Identity and notification solve different parts: the update tells Angular to check, and `track` tells Angular how existing views correspond to the new collection.

sections.title: List insertion with stable keys
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Old[Old keys: 10, 20, 30] --> Match[Match by task.id]
  New[New keys: 5, 10, 20, 30] --> Match
  Match --> Create[Create view for key 5]
  Match --> Reuse10[Reuse view for key 10]
  Match --> Reuse20[Move view for key 20]
  Match --> Reuse30[Move view for key 30]
```

questions.question: How do you prevent Observable subscription leaks when an Angular component is destroyed?
questions.title: Observable Subscription Cleanup
questions.direct_answer: Prefer `AsyncPipe` for template values because it manages its subscription, and use `takeUntilDestroyed` for imperative Observable work tied to a component or service lifetime. Manual subscriptions to long-lived sources must otherwise be unsubscribed; normal finite streams that complete release themselves.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `AsyncPipe` subscribes, renders the latest value, and unsubscribes on destroy.
`takeUntilDestroyed()` completes a pipeline when its injection context is destroyed.
Pass a `DestroyRef` when `takeUntilDestroyed` is called outside an injection context.
Long-lived intervals, sockets, and shared event streams need a cleanup boundary.
A completed Observable closes its subscription, but cancellation may still matter earlier.

sections.title: Interview answer
Subscription lifetime and component destruction
sections.content:
An Observable describes how values reach an observer. Calling `subscribe` creates a subscription, and that relationship stays active until the source completes, errors, or the subscription is cancelled. A destroyed Angular component does not automatically cancel every subscription created manually in its class.

`AsyncPipe` owns the subscription for a template binding. It subscribes to the current Observable or Promise, provides the latest value, notifies Angular when the value changes, and cleans up on component destruction. If the expression begins returning a different Observable, it switches subscriptions safely. This makes the template and lifetime owner visible in one place.

`takeUntilDestroyed` fits class logic that must react imperatively. During component construction, the operator can obtain the current `DestroyRef` from dependency injection. When that context is destroyed, the pipeline completes. A helper called later can receive an explicitly captured `DestroyRef`.

An interval, WebSocket, router event stream, or shared subject may never complete on its own and therefore needs this boundary. A one-response HTTP stream normally completes, but unsubscribing can still cancel a request when navigation makes its result irrelevant. Cleanup is not a ritual applied blindly to every Observable; it is part of defining who owns the work and how long that work remains useful.

sections.title: Observable ownership and cleanup paths
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Source[Observable source] --> Use{How is the value consumed?}
  Use -->|template value| Async[AsyncPipe subscription]
  Use -->|imperative effect| Operator[takeUntilDestroyed pipeline]
  Async --> Destroy[Component destroyed]
  Operator --> Destroy
  Destroy --> Close[Subscription removed]
  Source -->|completes first| Complete[Subscription closes normally]
```
